entry.title: Giving teeth to expected EC disabling: P2XX(-T)(-ML)
entry.summary:
The discussion centers on the selection process for the base point coordinates (G) of the secp256k1 curve used in Bitcoin cryptography. The initial assumption that G was chosen using a specific method is debated, with a clarification that this might not be the case based on existing knowledge and references such as detailed in a [Bitcoin Stack Exchange post](https://bitcoin.stackexchange.com/questions/58784/how-were-the-secp256k1-base-point-coordinates-decided). It highlights the possibility that the method of choosing G may still hold some uncertainties.
There's a proposal to consider tweaking the hash function by incorporating more recent and unbiased data, such as the hash of Bitcoin's genesis block or the hash of the first block where a new protocol, referred to as 'canary,' is implemented. This suggestion credits Tadge Dryja for the idea, indicating a collaborative approach in the ongoing development and security enhancement of cryptographic methods.
Moreover, the email touches upon the limitations of batching Shor's algorithm for multi-target attacks within cryptographic contexts, suggesting that employing Merkle Tree-Encoded Digital Signature Algorithm (MT-ECDLP) might simplify rather than complicate classical attacks like Grover's search. This technical insight into cryptographic resistance strategies against potential quantum computing threats underscores the complexities and challenges faced in securing blockchain technology.
